title: The Overtoaster
pitch: The product page, control panel and manual of an invented heater-grid toaster that burns pictures onto bread, with a real two-stage heat and moisture simulation underneath. The visitor sets power per heating cell, watches the slice dry out first and only then brown, and tries to match a daily target design without charring the crust, while the product's absurd subscription tiers and pop-ups pester the page in the margins. The finished slice is a screenshot-ready piece of burnt art with a deadpan review.
whyNow: Timeless. Appliances that hide features behind paywalls and apps are a lasting genre to lampoon, and a toaster is the oldest joke in connected gadgets.

research.summary: Search re-checks agree on the physics that shapes the mechanic: bread surface water holds the surface near or below 100 C, so toasting is a drying stage followed by a browning stage. Sources disagree on when browning starts (about 120 to 150 C in a patent summary, about 140 C in a science explainer, above about 155 C in an encyclopedia article), so the sim uses a labelled toy band. Patents and older gadgets already print or select browning patterns, including heat-blocking plates and a PC-connected 2008 concept, so the page is a genre parody and not a novelty claim. Press and commentary pages describe hardware features moved behind subscriptions (a car-maker garage opener, a baby bassinet), which grounds the tier-and-pop-up satire; the page targets the practice and names no company.

facts.claim: Sources differ on when toast browning starts: about 120 to 150 C in a patent summary, about 140 C in a science explainer, above about 155 C in an encyclopedia article.
Water in the bread surface holds the surface at or below about 100 C until it evaporates, so toasting runs as a drying stage and then a browning stage; the patent says the drying can take minutes.
Pattern-browning toasters have been patented, including a swappable heat-blocking plate design (US7290482) and older pattern-plate patents.

The 2008 Scan Toaster was a PC-connected design concept, covered by The Register and TechCrunch, that used movable heated modules to burn weather or headlines onto bread; no mass production was reported in that coverage.
Press and commentary pages describe hardware features moved behind subscriptions, with a car-maker garage opener and a baby bassinet as examples.

design.coreLoop: The visitor picks a bread slice and a target design, sets power on a heater grid of cells (paint, drag or choose presets) and a timer, and presses start. A 2D simulation heats the slice, dries it, then browns it, with a heat-map overlay and a scrubbable replay. Score compares the finished slice to the target and penalises char; a deadpan review and a screenshot card close the round. A seeded daily target and tightening limits (fewer cells, shorter time) keep later attempts different, while the satire layer adds playful interruptions such as a tier upsell that never blocks the controls.
sophisticationHooks: Coupled moisture and temperature fields with a drying plateau near 100 C, browning accumulating in a 120 to 155 C band and char beyond it, so the physics itself teaches patience
Heater-grid painter with a live heat-map overlay and replay scrubber
Deadpan satire shell: product page with invented firmware tiers, a cookie-consent banner about the crust, a manual and a generated review of your toast
Seeded daily target drawn in code, URL-hash share of the power map, canvas export of the finished slice and synthesized crackle and ding
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: about 40 by 30 field simulation on canvas with fixed-step update, heater-grid editor with presets, about 12 code-drawn target stencils, scoring with char penalty, replay scrubber from stored frames, product page, manual, tier and consent parody that never block controls, daily seed and hash share, light/dark, reduced motion, keyboard and touch, about panel. Cut: image upload, multi-slice batches, extended audio (one crackle and one ding only), any real electrical-safety advice. Fallback if time runs short: drop the replay scrubber and keep the final heat-map.
risks: Image-toasting gadgets and patents (heat-blocking plates, a 2008 PC-connected concept, an app-controlled toaster) already exist, so novelty rests on the physics sim and the satire shell, not on toast art.
Browning thresholds vary by source (about 120 to 155 C); the page presents a simplified toy band labelled as an estimate, not science advice.

Claim not verified: whether any appliance maker is moving toaster-class features behind subscriptions. The page will not state it; the tiers are plainly invented, and any mention is shown as 'as of 2026-10-10, per the Boing Boing post' or omitted.
Claim not verified: the current availability of the Toasteroid and any owner backlash over the garage opener. The page omits both.
Pop-up satire must not obstruct the controls or hide instructions; mitigate with non-modal, dismissible, keyboard-reachable gags.
Subscription satire targets the practice only; no real company, product or logo appears on the page, and the fictional maker is labelled as such.
Frame rate on small phones; mitigate with a small grid, fixed-step update and a reduced grid on narrow screens.

verification.notes: Physics and genre-prior-art claims were found again by claim searches (WebFetch of patents.google.com failed on DNS); four sources (Fatherly, PIRG, Techdirt, Torque News) did not come back and were replaced or dropped, and the unverified appliance-subscription claim was removed. Scope was trimmed to a 40 by 30 grid and about 12 stencils to leave room for QA.
